title: Inventions That Changed The World
author: Catherine Baker
source: FFT Tutoring with the Lightning Squad (tutoring.fft.org.uk), screenshots supplied 6 Oct 2026

pages.heading: Inspiring Inventions
pages.text: There are lots of cool inventions that we take for granted in our daily lives. For example, when you get back from school, you might pop a slice of bread in the toaster for a quick snack. Maybe you use a computer or tablet to do some research for your homework. Then perhaps you settle down to watch TV or play a computer game. Only 150 years ago, however, none of those things would have been possible, because toasters, computers, tablets and televisions hadn’t been invented. These inventions all seem very ordinary to us now, but they changed the world! There are many fascinating stories behind common inventions – and many different reasons why they were invented in the first place. Let’s read on to learn about some of these inventions and the stories behind them.

pages.heading: Invented To Solve a Problem
pages.text: Inventors are often inspired by a problem that they need to solve. There are many examples of this, but the story of Chester Greenwood shows that you don’t have to be an adult to come up with a useful invention! Chester was just 15 years old when he invented earmuffs, back in 1873. He had the idea when he was ice skating outdoors, in freezing winter weather. In those days, most people wore woollen caps to keep their ears warm, but Chester found those too itchy. Apparently, when he got back from his skating trip, he asked his grandmother to make a wire frame like a headband, with warm, fluffy pads at each end. Chester kept tinkering with the design of his earmuffs, and in the end, they became so popular that he built a factory near his home to make them!

pages.heading: New Uses for Old Inventions
pages.text: Sometimes it can take a while to find the right use for an invention. Back in 1968, a researcher called Spencer Silver was trying to invent a new kind of extra-strong glue. He didn’t have much luck with that. However, by accident, he ended up inventing a new type of glue that stuck things together very lightly, so you could peel them apart and reposition them. This meant you could remove the thing you’d glued on, if you wanted to, and not damage whatever it was stuck on. For ages, he tried to convince people that his invention was useful, but no one really believed him.

pages.heading: New Uses for Old Inventions
pages.text: It wasn’t until 1980, 12 years later, that Spencer’s colleague, Arthur Fry, came up with a brilliant idea for using Spencer’s glue. Arthur liked to use scraps of paper to mark the pages in his music book, but they often fell out of the book. He tried putting Spencer’s glue on the paper scraps. The scraps stayed in the book, and they didn’t damage the pages if they ever needed to be moved around. Together, Spencer and Arthur had invented sticky notes!

pages.heading: Learning From Nature
pages.text: Some inventors have been inspired by ideas they found in nature. This is what happened to George de Mestral. Back in 1948, George went for a walk in the woods with his dog. He noticed that lots of spiky, little seeds called burrs got caught in his clothes, and in his dog’s fur. It was surprisingly hard to pull the burrs off!

pages.heading: Learning From Nature
pages.text: George took a close look at the burrs under a microscope. He noticed that the burrs’ spikes ended in a hook. That meant they easily got caught in the loops of clothing fabric or fur. George realised that he could use this idea to make a new way of fastening clothes – where one side of the fastener had little hooks, and the other side had loops. George’s invention – Velcro® - is still used today on shoe straps, and as fasteners on coats, gloves and mittens.

pages.heading: A Life-Saving Invention
pages.text: In 1965, Stephanie Kwolek was part of a team trying to produce a new type of fibre. The team wanted to invent a fibre strong enough that even sharp spikes and bullets wouldn’t break through it. It wasn’t easy to discover how to make this new fibre, but Stephanie kept working away at the problem. She did many different experiments, and eventually she invented a new material that was unlike anything else that came before it.

pages.heading: A Life-Saving Invention
pages.text: She called her invention - Kevlar® - a fibre five times stronger than steel! Today, Kevlar saves people’s lifes! It is used in body armour such as bulletproof vests. It’s also used to make safety helmets that protect people’s heads when they are doing dangerous sports and building work. It’s in a lot of other products too, from gloves and sports equipment to tyres and tennis rackets.

pages.heading: Always Changing
pages.text: Some inventions keep on changing! One invention that has changed many people’s lives for the better is the telephone. The telephone was originally invented about 150 years ago by Alexander Graham Bell. However, it wasn’t until the 1930s, that wealthier people in the UK started to have their own phones at home. These early phones were plugged into the wall, so you had to stay in one place if you wanted to use them. In the 1980s, the cordless telephone was invented, so you could walk around as you chatted, but you still couldn’t use your phone outside your house.

pages.heading: Always Changing
pages.text: Mobile phones first started to become popular in the 1990s, and they allowed people to make phone calls from wherever they were. Early mobiles were quite basic, with small black and white screens for making phone calls, sending texts and playing very simple games. The invention of smartphone in the early 2000s changed everything though. For the first time, people could use the internet, play music and games, take photos, and have video calls with their friends, all from the same small, handheld phone. Alexander Graham Bell would be amazed at how far his invention has come!

glossary.inspired: Given an idea or the wish to do something.
glossary.apparently: It seems so, from what people say.
glossary.tinkering: Making small changes to improve something.
glossary.reposition: Move something to a different place.
glossary.microscope: An instrument that makes tiny things look much bigger.
glossary.fibre: A thin thread, used to make cloth and other materials.
